'''Gilbert Stork''' (December 31, 1921 – October 21, 2017)<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nakamura|first1=Eiichi|last2=Winkler|first2=Jeffrey D.|last3=Aggarwal|first3=Varinder K.|s2cid=1109751|title=Gilbert Stork (1921–2017)|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition|volume=57|issue=1|language=en|doi=10.1002/anie.201711474|pmid=29193592|issn=1521-3773|year=2018|page=36|doi-access=free}}</ref> was a Belgian-American [[organic chemistry|organic chemist]]. For a quarter of a century he was the Eugene Higgins Professor of Chemistry [[Professor Emeritus|Emeritus]] at [[Columbia University]].<ref name="Hargittai">{{cite book|last1=Hargittai|first1=István|last2=Hargittai|first2=Magdolna|title=More conversations with famous chemists|date=2003|publisher=Imperial College Press|location=London|isbn=978-1-86094-336-2|pages=109–119|edition=[Verschiedene Aufl.]|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_uu3CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA109|access-date=December 1, 2016}}</ref> He is known for making significant contributions to the [[total synthesis]] of [[natural product]]s, including a lifelong fascination with the synthesis of [[quinine]]. In so doing he also made a number of contributions to mechanistic understanding of reactions, and performed pioneering work on [[enamine]] chemistry, leading to development of the [[Stork enamine alkylation]].<ref name="Hargittai" />{{rp|111}}<ref name="Terrell">{{cite journal|last1=Stork|first1=Gilbert|title=A New Synthesis of 2-Alkyl and 2-Acyl Ketones|last2=Terrell|first2=Ross|last3=Szmuszkovicz|first3=Jacob|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=April 1954|volume=76|issue=7|pages=2029–2030|doi=10.1021/ja01636a103|bibcode=1954JAChS..76.2029S }}</ref>
It is believed he was responsible for the first planned stereocontrolled synthesis as well as the first natural product to be synthesised with high stereoselectivity.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Seeman|first=Jeffrey I.|s2cid=42348686|date=March 19, 2012|title=Gilbert Stork: In His Own Words and in the Musings of His Friends|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition|language=en|volume=51|issue=12|pages=3012–3023|doi=10.1002/anie.201200033|pmid=22383434|issn=1521-3773}}</ref>

Stork was also a mentor of young chemists with many of his students going on to make significant contributions in their own right.

== Early life ==
Gilbert Stork was born in the [[Ixelles]] municipality of [[Brussels, Belgium]] on December 31, 1921.<ref name="reminiscences">{{cite journal|last1=Stork|first1=Gilbert|title=Chemical reminiscences|journal=Tetrahedron|date=December 2011|volume=67|issue=51|pages=9754–9764|doi=10.1016/j.tet.2011.10.007|url=http://doc.sciencenet.cn/upload/file/201229164333861.pdf|access-date=December 1, 2016|archive-date=December 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201211102/http://doc.sciencenet.cn/upload/file/201229164333861.pdf|url-status=dead}}{{open access}}</ref><ref name="Top">{{cite journal|title=C&EN's Top 75|journal=Chemical and Engineering News|date=January 12, 1998|url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/hotarticles/cenear/980112/top.html|access-date=December 1, 2016}}</ref> The oldest of 3 children, his middle brother Michel died in infancy, but he remained close with his younger sister Monique his whole life.  His family had Jewish origins, although Gilbert himself didn't recall them being religiously active.<ref name="reminiscences" /> The family moved to [[Nice]] when Gilbert was about 14 (circa. 1935) and remained there until 1939. During this period, Gilbert completed his [[lycée]] studies, distinguishing himself in French literature and writing. Characterizing himself during those years as "not terribly self-confident," and uncertain whether he could find employment in a profession he enjoyed, Gilbert considered applying for a colonial civil service job in [[French Indochina]].<ref name=":0" /> However, the outbreak of World War II that year led the family to flee to New York, where his father's older brother, Sylvain, had already emigrated.

== Education ==
Gilbert studied for a Bachelor of Science at the [[University of Florida]], from 1940 to 1942. He then moved to the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] for this PhD, which he obtained in 1945 under the supervision of [[Samuel M. McElvain]].<ref name="Wisconsin">{{cite web|title=UW Madison Chemistry Newsletter for February 17, 2014 Mon|url=https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/uw-madison-chemistry-newsletter-2172014|website=University of Wisconsin|access-date=February 17, 2014|archive-date=December 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201143915/https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/uw-madison-chemistry-newsletter-2172014|url-status=dead}}</ref> While at Wisconsin he met [[Carl Djerassi]], with whom he would go on to form a lasting friendship.

== Career ==
* 1946 [[Harvard University]]: Instructor; 1948 Assistant Professor
* 1953 Columbia University: Associate Professor; 1955 Professor; 1967–1993 Eugene Higgins Professor; *1993 Professor Emeritus<ref name="Hoffman">{{cite journal|last1=Hoffman|first1=Frances|title=Gilbert Stork: A Celebration of 35 Years in Research & Teaching|journal=Aldrichimica Acta|date=1982|volume=15|pages=1–10}}</ref>

== Elected to ==
* U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]], 1961
* [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], 1962
* Foreign Member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]], 1989
* [[American Philosophical Society]], 1995<ref name="Columbia">{{cite journal|title=Faculty Named to Learned Society|journal=Columbia University Record|date=May 17, 1995|volume=20|issue=29|url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/record/archives/vol20/vol20_iss29/record2029.15.html|access-date=December 1, 2016}}</ref>
* The [[Royal Society]], UK 1999

== Incidents ==

=== The explosive steak ===
During his time at the University of Wisconsin, Stork kept a steak on his windowsill in the winter in order to keep it refrigerated. The steak began to degrade and to dispose of it Stork put it in a hot acid bath used to clean glassware which contained nitric and sulphuric acids. He was then concerned he would produce [[nitroglycerin]]e due to the glycerine in the steak and the presence of nitric and sulphuric acids. However, due to the high temperature of the bath, the oxidation of glycerol was much faster than the nitration of glycerin thus preventing the formation of explosives.<ref name=":0" />

== Awards ==
Professor Stork received a number of awards and honors including the following:<ref name="Japan">{{cite web|title=Emeritus Professor Gilbert Stork (Columbia University) was awarded an honorary member from the Chemical Society of Japan.|url=http://www.chem.s.u-tokyo.ac.jp/~common/stork/StorkE.html|website=Chemical Society of Japan|access-date=December 1, 2016}}</ref>

{{div col|colwidth=35em}}
* 1957 [[ACS Award in pure chemistry|Award in Pure Chemistry]] of the American Chemical Society
* 1959 [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|Guggenheim Foundation]] Fellow
* 1961 Baekeland Medal, North Jersey ACS
* 1962 Harrison Howe Award
* 1966 Edward Curtis Franklin Memorial Award, Stanford University
* 1967 ACS Award for Creative Work in Synthetic Organic Chemistry
* 1971 Synthetic Organic Chemical Manufacturers Association Gold Medal
* 1973 Nebraska Award
* 1978 Roussel Prize, Paris
* 1980 Nichols Medal, New York ACS, [[Arthur C. Cope Award]], ACS
* 1982 Edgar Fahs Smith Award, Philadelphia ACS
* 1982 [[Willard Gibbs Medal]], Chicago ACS
* 1982 [[NAS Award in Chemical Sciences|National Academy of Sciences Award in Chemical Sciences]]
* 1982 [[National Medal of Science]] from [[Ronald Reagan]];<ref name="reminiscences" /> [[Linus Pauling Award]]
* 1985 [[Tetrahedron Prize]]
* 1986 [[Remsen Award]], Maryland ACS<ref name="Maryland Section 2018">{{cite web | title=Ira Remsen Award | website=Maryland Section | date=November 14, 2018 | url=https://maryland.sites.acs.org/remsenaward.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181114143228/https://maryland.sites.acs.org/remsenaward.htm | archive-date=November 14, 2018 | url-status=live | access-date=November 14, 2018}}</ref>
* 1986 Cliff S. Hamilton Award
* 1987 Monie A Ferst Award and Medal, [[Georgia Institute of Technology|Georgia Tech]].
* 1991 Roger Adams Award
* 1992 George Kenner Award, Liverpool
* 1992 Robert Robinson Lectureship, [[University of Manchester]]
* 1992 [[Chemical Pioneer Award]], [[American Institute of Chemists]]
* 1993 [[Welch Award in Chemistry]], [[Robert A. Welch Foundation]]
* 1994 Allan R. Day Award, Philadelphia Organic Chemists Club
* 1995 [[Wolf Prize]], Israel
* 2002 Sir Derek Barton Gold medal, [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]
* 2005 Herbert C. Brown Award, [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name="Morris" />
{{div col end}}

Stork also held [[honorary doctorates]] from [[Lawrence University]], the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], the [[University of Paris]], the [[University of Rochester]], and [[Columbia University]].<ref name="Morris">{{cite news|last1=Morris|first1=Colin|title=Chemistry Department Continues Award-Winning Legacy|url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/news/04/10/chemistry.html|access-date=December 1, 2016|work=Columbia News|date=January 10, 2005}}</ref><ref name="Richardson">{{cite news|last1=Richardson|first1=Lynda|title=COMMENCEMENTS; Columbia Chief Stresses Role of Teacher|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/05/20/nyregion/commencements-columbia-chief-stresses-role-of-teacher.html|access-date=December 1, 2016|work=The New York Times|date=May 20, 1993}}</ref>

The inaugural Gilbert Stork Lecture was held in his honor in 2014 at his alma mater, the University of Wisconsin-Madison.<ref name="Hargittai" /><ref name="Lecture">{{cite news|title=Seminars|url=https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/uw-madison-chemistry-newsletter-10272014|access-date=December 1, 2016|work=UW Madison Chemistry Newsletter|date=October 27, 2014|archive-date=December 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201143941/https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/uw-madison-chemistry-newsletter-10272014|url-status=dead}}</ref> Gilbert Stork named lecture series are also held at other institutions, including [[Columbia University]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Named Lecture The Gilbert Stork Lecture|url=http://chem.columbia.edu/events/named-lecture/the-gilbert-stork-lecture/|website=Columbia University|access-date=December 1, 2016|archive-date=June 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160620185310/http://chem.columbia.edu/events/named-lecture/the-gilbert-stork-lecture/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[University of Pennsylvania]], as a result of his endowments.<ref>{{cite web|title=Gilbert Stork Lecture|url=https://www.chem.upenn.edu/events/named-lecture-series/gilbert-stork-lecture|website=University of Pennsylvania|access-date=December 1, 2016}}</ref>

He was fêted for his sense of humor and colorful personality by historian of chemistry [[Jeffrey I. Seeman]] who published a collection of "Storkisms".<ref name="Halford">{{cite web|last1=Halford|first1=Bethany|title=Gilbert Stork on How Not to Dispose of a Steak|url=http://cenblog.org/newscripts/2012/03/gilbert-stork-on-how-not-to-dispose-of-a-steak/|website=The Safety Zone|access-date=March 6, 2012|date=March 6, 2012}}</ref>
